finding.title: Drain loop memoization couples correctness to object identity; state corruption on bundle reuse
finding.summary: The advanceAudit drain loop (src/audit/orchestrator/advance.ts, lines 320-360) memoizes deriveAuditState results via WeakMap keyed on ArtifactBundle object identity. The design assumes bundle identity ALWAYS changes on every transition (line 235: `const finalizedBundle = { ...metadataBundle, ...}`). This is a BEHAVIORAL CONTRACT, not enforced by types. If any refactor reuses a bundle (via conditional path or executor mutation), the memoization cache silently returns STALE state for downstream obligations. This causes silent mis-decisions in the drain loop—the system computes wrong obligation sets, halts incorrectly, or skips valid work. The bug is invisible until that specific refactor or load pattern triggers bundle reuse. Removing memoization costs ~8-9x per-iteration deriveAuditState calls, but the current design trades performance for a latent correctness defect. This is adversarial-scale risk: structural code changes can silently introduce state corruption.

finding.title: File-lock timeout coupling creates deadlock window; concurrent holders clobber state.json
finding.summary: LockedJsonStore (src/shared/io/lockedJsonStore.ts, lines 14-15) derives acquisition timeout as STALE_LOCK_MS - 10_000ms to avoid stale-lock collisions. If a process holding the lock CRASHES between writing the lock file and releasing it, the lock sits for up to 30s. Multiple concurrent holders will timeout at 20s, assume the lock is stale, and ALL proceed simultaneously, clobbering each other's writes to state.json. The 10s safety margin is insufficient under high load or slow filesystems. On fast-iteration CI or large audit runs with many workers, concurrent timeouts become measurable. Result: corrupted state.json, lost work, silent data loss. The coupling is intentional but the failure mode is undetectable until it occurs.

finding.title: Token quota estimates never re-validated against actual usage; budget overruns cascade across waves
finding.summary: The quota scheduler (src/shared/quota/scheduler.ts) derives token budgets from estimateTokensFromBytes (file-size heuristics), but actual usage is recorded AFTER dispatch via response headers. If actual usage is 2x the estimate (cached request returns fewer tokens, LLM tokenization differs), the scheduler's NEXT wave has wrongly budgeted. The system does NOT re-plan in-flight work when it detects overage—it simply records it and continues. This cascades: wave 1 uses 2x budget → reported overages aren't reflected in wave 2 → wave 2 dispatches beyond capacity → 429/524 errors. Quota source is reactive, not predictive. Errors compound across multi-wave audits. Early over-estimation accumulates into late dispatch that exceeds all remaining quota, leaving work undone.

finding.summary: MAX_DRAIN_STEPS (advance.ts, line 48) is set to 64; loop halts when cap is reached, returning current state WITHOUT throwing or escalating. finding.title: Obligation state derivation split across 596-line file with implicit staleness dependencies
finding.summary: src/audit/orchestrator/state.ts (596 lines) computes obligation states checking artifact presence/staleness across ~40 obligations, each with different rules. Single reused staleOrSatisfied() function, but staleness DAG rules are implicit: 'file_disposition depends on file_disposition.json', 'charter_delta_current depends on charter_register', etc. Developer changing staleness rules must understand entire dependency graph mentally. File has no visual structure—long series of `obligations.push()` calls. Mathematician notes obligation DAG ordering (P3-008) is enforced only through code review—no compile-time validation. If someone reorders PRIORITY entries without understanding graph, pipeline silently breaks (e.g., charter_extraction before intent_checkpoint_current). Requires tracing data dependencies manually through 60+ lines.

finding.title: Artifact staleness DAG: sophisticated optimization but high cognitive overhead, questionable payoff
finding.summary: Audit maintains explicit staleness dependency map (src/audit/orchestrator/staleness.ts, artifactMetadata.ts) so upstream artifact changes mark downstream dependents stale. Logic tracks semantic hashes, metadata migration, dependency ordering, flow coverage baselines. Theoretically sound but creates complexity: artifact recomputation threads through staleness checks, tests mock artifact freshness, new artifacts require careful DAG insertion. Pragmatist question: does real-world payoff justify complexity? Most users probably don't care about maximal artifact reuse; simpler strategy (regenerate everything on resume, or use file modification time) would be less to maintain. Staleness system is OPTIMIZATION, not requirement. Cost of removing: ~8-9x deriveAuditState calls per iteration.

finding.title: Charter extraction, delta, and clarification are three sequential passes; consolidation opportunity
finding.summary: The charter layer runs three sequential passes: (1) charter_extraction_executor assembles charters from the consensus scaffold (Phase C.1); (2) charter_delta_executor independently mines deltas (Phase C.2, deliberately separate so it doesn't mark its own homework); (3) charter_clarification_executor runs the triangulation loop to resolve open questions (Phase D). Each is a separate obligation, separate executor, separate host-delegation round. While the independence of the delta-mining pass is architecturally sound (adversarial second-pass), the three passes could potentially be coordinated as a single umbrella obligation with internal phase gating (extract → delta → clarify) rather than three external obligation gates. Benefit: cleaner obligation frontier (fewer states before planning), simpler state machine. Drawback: less granular pause/resume control if one phase takes a long time. Current design optimizes for pause-ability at phase boundaries; consolidated design optimizes for simplicity.

finding.title: Design review contract and conceptual passes plus second-order challenge are three independent loops; unified loop opportunity
finding.summary: The design review layer runs three distinct loops: (1) design_review_contract (audit-findings contract assessment); (2) design_review_conceptual (conceptual design critique); (3) systemic_challenge_executor (second-order adversary, loop-until-dry). Each is scheduled as a separate obligation and invokes the host-delegation dispatch independently. All three are ADVISORY FINDINGS (leads, not verdicts) and all three consume host quota via the dispatch broker. The current design allows each to run independently and potentially in different dispatch rounds. Opportunity: unify all three as a single "design_review_unified" obligation that internally orchestrates contract → conceptual → challenge with consistent loop-until-dry termination (all three converge together rather than individually). Benefit: single dispatch coordination, clearer resource budgeting, stronger convergence properties. Drawback: less independent scheduling flexibility, larger single dispatch packet. The comment on systemic_challenge says "loop-until-dry second-order adversary pass" but the loop itself is implicit in the obligation re-firing; explicit loop orchestration at the unified level could be clearer.

finding.summary: Audit implements language-neutral dependency graph extraction via 12+ manifest-edge parsers (src/audit/extractors/graphManifestEdges/: cargo.ts, go.ts, jsonc.ts, maven.ts, packageJson.ts, pnpm.ts, pyproject.ts, toml.ts, typescript.ts, workspace.ts, yaml.ts, yamlPaths.ts) plus heuristic extraction. Alternative (acquire language-specific tools—Cargo, Maven, npm, Poetry—and normalize output) might be simpler than maintaining dozen custom parsers. Current approach is admirable but adds hundreds of lines for functionality rarely used in practice.

finding.title: Test-to-code 1:1 ratio (516 source / 557 test files) suggests inherent complexity, not simplicity
finding.summary: Codebase has 516 TypeScript source files in src/ and 557 test files in tests/—1:1 ratio. This is high and suggests inherent complexity requiring extensive testing for correctness. Simpler systems typically have 1:3 or 1:4 source-to-test ratio. Ratio not inherently bad, but indicates architecture is not simple—every feature has corresponding tests suggesting behavior is non-obvious. If design were simpler, test burden would be lower. Suggests room for architectural simplification.
